title: Reading: summary completion and sentence endings
status: Private teacher-review revision DRAFT v1.1.0 (NOT approved or released; prior v1.0.0 approval is historical only).
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional draft, AI-assisted. Passages are original and describe general, widely reported trends without citing specific studies, operators or figures. Human editorial, factual, key, mapping, difficulty and originality review pending.
prerequisites: Lesson 6 (reading for specific information) and Lesson 9 (headings and the writer's argument).
Teacher has checked actual Reading Screener and review states privately.
Optional extension: use when learners need more practice with summary and sentence-ending tasks.

objectives.text: Locate the part of a passage that a summary covers and use the order of information to find each answer.
Choose words that fit both the grammar and the meaning of a summary gap, copying passage words exactly and respecting the word limit.
Match sentence beginnings with endings that are true according to the passage, rejecting endings that are true only in general.

levels.foundation: Word-type hints beside each gap; the teacher marks where each summary starts; sort box words by word type before choosing.
levels.core: Complete all fifteen questions in the time given, with correct spelling and word limits.
levels.extension: Underline the summary words that paraphrase the passage and name the distractor for each box question.
levels.high_band: Independently complete a fresh unfamiliar passage under a strict timer. For every incorrect option, cite a specific contradiction, unsupported assumption, or grammar mismatch; explain the writer's qualified position without relying on copied wording.

blocks.title: Grammar fit or meaning fit?
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; learners choose before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Gap: 'Many sleeper routes closed because cheap ______ made them unprofitable.' Three learners chose different words. Which answer is right, and what went wrong in the other two?

examples.label: Answer A
examples.comment: Grammar fails: after the adjective 'cheap' the gap needs a noun. Always say the whole sentence with your word in it.

examples.label: Answer B
examples.comment: Grammar fits, but 'airlines' is not in the passage. In a 'words from the passage' summary, the answer must be copied from the text.

examples.label: Answer C
examples.comment: Correct: a noun, taken from the passage ('Cheap flights could carry passengers'), and it makes the meaning of the summary true.

blocks.title: Summary completion: words from the passage
blocks.mode: Guided practice; answer alone, then check with a partner
blocks.instructions: Read the passage. Complete the summary of paragraphs 1-3. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

stimulus.title: The quiet return of the night train
paragraphs: For much of the late twentieth century, the overnight sleeper train seemed to belong to the past. Cheap flights could carry passengers between distant cities in a couple of hours, and many rail companies decided that the cost of running trains with beds, staff and restaurant cars could no longer be justified. Across Europe, one route after another was withdrawn, and the carriages were sold or left to rust in sidings.

In recent years, however, the night train has made an unexpected return. Several operators have reopened routes that had been closed for decades, and some have ordered new carriages for the first time in a generation. The main reason is a change in how travellers think about flying. A growing number of people, particularly younger travellers, are looking for ways to reduce the carbon emissions from their journeys, and a train that leaves in the evening and arrives the next morning offers a practical alternative for distances of up to about fifteen hundred kilometres.

Supporters also point to a hidden advantage: time. A flight may last only two hours, but once the journey to the airport, security checks and waiting are included, the total can easily reach six or seven. A night train, by contrast, departs from the city centre and arrives in another city centre, and the hours spent travelling are hours that would otherwise be spent asleep in a hotel. For business travellers in particular, this can mean a full working day at the destination without the cost of an extra night's accommodation.

The revival has not been easy. Sleeper carriages are expensive to build and can make only one journey every twenty-four hours, so each one earns far less than a daytime train. Tickets, especially for private compartments, are often more expensive than flights on the same route. Operators have also struggled with the practical problems of crossing borders, where differences in electrical systems, signalling and safety rules may require a change of locomotive or even of staff.

Whether night trains can grow beyond a small, enthusiastic market will depend largely on decisions by governments. Some have offered support in the form of reduced track charges or direct subsidies, arguing that the environmental benefits justify public money. Others remain unconvinced, pointing out that the same funds could improve daytime services used by far more people. For now, the night train is no longer a relic, but nor is it yet a serious rival to the aeroplane.

blocks.form_title: Summary: why night trains declined and returned

items.prompt: An important factor behind the withdrawal of sleeper services was competition from low-cost ______.
items.evidence: Cheap flights could carry passengers between distant cities
items.reason: 'Cheap' before the gap tells you a noun is needed; the passage gives 'flights'.

items.prompt: Old carriages were sold or left to rust in ______.
items.evidence: the carriages were sold or left to rust in sidings
items.reason: The summary keeps the passage's own words; copy the spelling exactly.

items.prompt: Many travellers now want to cut the carbon ______ produced by their journeys.
items.evidence: reduce the carbon emissions from their journeys
items.reason: 'Cut' paraphrases 'reduce'; the noun after 'carbon' is the answer.

items.prompt: Unlike airports, both ends of a sleeper journey can be in the urban ______.
items.evidence: departs from the city centre and arrives in another city centre
items.reason: 'Leaves from' paraphrases 'departs from'. One word only: not 'city centre'.

items.prompt: Business travellers can avoid paying for an extra night's ______.
items.evidence: without the cost of an extra night's accommodation
items.reason: 'Avoid paying for' paraphrases 'without the cost of'. Check the double 'c' and double 'm'.

blocks.support: Foundation: word-type hints are printed beside each gap; the teacher shows where paragraph 1 ends before learners start.
blocks.extension: For each answer, underline the words in the summary that paraphrase the passage. Advanced transfer: before revealing the key, require a cited justification of one correct response and one plausible incorrect response.

blocks.title: Summary completion: choosing from a box
blocks.mode: Independent practice under time (6 minutes); then check
blocks.instructions: Complete the summary of paragraphs 4-5 using the list of words, A-H, below. Write the correct letter. Three words are not used.

stimulus.title: Words: The quiet return of the night train
paragraphs: A  cheaper
B  government
C  slowly
D  borders
E  expensive
F  passengers
G  profitable
H  weather

items.prompt: The limitation on daily journeys makes each sleeper carriage relatively less ______.
items.evidence: each one earns far less than a daytime train
items.reason: 'Earns far less' means it is less profitable. Box words are often paraphrases, not copies.

items.prompt: Tickets for private compartments are frequently more ______ than air travel.
items.evidence: are often more expensive than flights on the same route
items.reason: 'Cheaper' is the opposite trap: the passage says tickets cost more.

items.prompt: Crossing ______ causes technical and staffing problems.
items.evidence: the practical problems of crossing borders
items.reason: Electrical systems, signalling and staff change at borders.

items.prompt: The future of night trains depends mostly on ______ decisions.
items.evidence: will depend largely on decisions by governments
items.reason: 'Mostly' paraphrases 'largely'; 'decisions by governments' becomes 'government decisions'.

items.prompt: Critics say the money would help more ______ if it were spent on daytime services.
items.evidence: daytime services used by far more people
items.reason: 'People' who use trains are passengers; the box gives the paraphrase.

blocks.support: Foundation: before reading, sort the eight box words into nouns and adjectives; each gap then has fewer candidates.
blocks.high_band: Explain in one sentence why A (cheaper) and C (slowly) are attractive wrong answers.

blocks.title: Sentence endings
blocks.mode: Independent practice under time (6 minutes); then check
blocks.instructions: Use the passage 'The quiet return of the night train'. Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-H, below. Three endings are not used.

stimulus.title: Endings
paragraphs: A  because operators could not justify the running costs.
B  because the price of flights has risen sharply.
C  because each carriage can only be used once a day.
D  because they want to lower the environmental impact of their travel.
E  because trains are faster than planes.
F  because the money could benefit more people elsewhere.
G  because they leave from and arrive in city centres.
H  because rail staff refused to work at night.

items.prompt: Younger travellers are increasingly choosing night trains
items.evidence: are looking for ways to reduce the carbon emissions from their journeys
items.reason: Paragraph 2: 'environmental impact' paraphrases 'carbon emissions'.

items.prompt: Each sleeper carriage earns less than a daytime train
items.evidence: can make only one journey every twenty-four hours
items.reason: 'Once a day' paraphrases 'every twenty-four hours'.

items.prompt: Night trains can save business travellers time
items.evidence: departs from the city centre and arrives in another city centre
items.reason: There is no journey to and from an airport.

items.prompt: Some governments question public investment in sleeper services
items.evidence: the same funds could improve daytime services used by far more people
items.reason: 'Unwilling' paraphrases 'remain unconvinced'.

items.prompt: Many sleeper routes were withdrawn in the past
items.evidence: the cost of running trains with beds, staff and restaurant cars could no longer be justified
items.reason: Paragraph 1 gives the reason for the closures.

blocks.support: Foundation: the teacher crosses out one wrong ending with the class first (E: the passage says flights are faster).
blocks.extension: Check every ending for grammar too: each must complete the sentence correctly as well as truthfully.

stages.title: Opening challenge: grammar fit or meaning fit?
stages.student: Choose the best answer for the gap, then say what is wrong with the other two.
stages.teacher: Learners vote. Reveal the comments one at a time. Write two rules on the board: the word must fit the grammar; the word must make the summary true.
stages.say: A summary answer has to pass two tests: grammar and meaning.

stages.title: How summaries work
stages.student: Note the four steps: find where the summary starts in the passage; predict the word type; read around the paraphrase; copy the word exactly.
stages.teacher: Explain that summaries usually follow the order of the passage and often cover only some paragraphs. Show that the title of the summary helps locate it.
stages.say: Summaries usually follow the passage order, so one answer helps you find the next.
stages.check: Learners can say where the G1 summary starts in the passage.

stages.title: Guided: words from the passage
stages.student: Read the passage and complete Questions 1-5 alone.
stages.teacher: Allow 8 minutes. Foundation learners use the word-type hints. Circulate and ask "Is that word in the passage?"
stages.say: If your word is not in the passage, it cannot be the answer.
stages.check: Every learner has written five answers.

stages.title: Check and explain
stages.student: Check answers with a partner, then with the class. Mark spelling errors separately.
stages.teacher: Reveal one answer at a time. For Q4, show why 'city centre' breaks the word limit.
stages.say: One word only means one word only.

stages.title: Choosing from a box
stages.teacher: Model the first step: sort the box words by word type. Then time 6 minutes. No dictionaries.
stages.say: Box words are usually paraphrases. Look for the meaning, not the same word.

stages.title: Check the box summary
stages.student: Check answers and note which wrong option tempted you.
stages.teacher: Reveal. Discuss Q7: why "cheaper" is a trap.
stages.say: Opposites are common distractors in word boxes.
stages.check: Learners can explain the Q7 trap.

stages.title: Sentence endings
stages.teacher: Teach: find the sentence beginning in the passage first, then choose the ending that matches both meaning and grammar.
stages.say: Find the beginning first; the ending must be true for that beginning.

stages.title: Check endings
stages.student: Check answers. For each wrong answer, find the sentence in the passage that proves the right ending.
stages.teacher: Reveal. Ask why E and B are wrong (the passage says the opposite or says nothing).
stages.say: An ending can be true in the world but not in the passage.
stages.check: Learners can locate the evidence for two answers.

stages.title: My reading log
stages.student: Record each wrong answer as: wrong place, wrong word type, wrong meaning, or spelling.
stages.teacher: Note the error types learners actually record. No band conversion.
stages.say: Knowing why you were wrong is the fastest way to improve.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and take the homework.
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets. Record the fresh-check date.
stages.say: Next time, use the four steps without the teacher.

exit_ticket: The two tests every summary answer must pass:
What I do first in a sentence-endings task:
My target for the next reading task:
homework: Choose a short news article in English. Write a four-sentence summary of it with four gaps, and give it to a classmate to complete.
Record five words you misspelled in this lesson and practise them.
Complete only the Brains Heist reading practice your teacher actually assigns. Suggested time: about 25 minutes.

blocks.title: Restoring public clocks
blocks.mode: Withheld independent transfer; unseen passage; no hints or dictionary
blocks.instructions: Complete Questions 1–6 with ONE WORD ONLY from the passage.

stimulus.title: Restoring public clocks
paragraphs: Before accurate wristwatches became common, municipal clocks helped people coordinate factory shifts, railway departures and meetings. Their value was practical rather than merely decorative. Yet their mechanisms were difficult to keep synchronised. Temperature changes affected the movement of metal parts, and maintenance was occasionally postponed when councils reduced spending. Public timekeeping depended as much on sustained investment as on machinery.

During the twentieth century, cheaper personal timepieces reduced the need for a town clock. Some authorities removed damaged mechanisms while preserving their elaborate faces. Others disconnected the hands rather than let them display an increasingly inaccurate time. By the 1970s, many towers were protected mainly for architectural reasons, although the service they once provided was no longer essential.

Recently, a few councils have proposed making the clocks operational again. Advocates say a public clock helps someone whose phone battery is empty and offers a shared reference point in busy streets. However, the social benefit is difficult to measure. In one survey, most residents described the clock as important to local identity, yet few remembered checking it during the previous week. The researchers cautioned against interpreting expressed affection as proof of frequent use.

Restoration is rarely as straightforward as replacing a battery. In a coastal town, salt carried inland by sea air had corroded the metal gears. An electronic movement would have been cheaper to install. The heritage committee nevertheless approved repairs to the original mechanical system, arguing that the moving mechanism was part of the monument's historical value. Opponents warned that the decision would reduce funding available to the nearby library. The dispute was therefore not about conservation alone, but also about which public service should take priority.

Another approach combines old and new systems. The original gears remain, while an unobtrusive controller makes occasional adjustments to their timing. This can reduce visits from specialist engineers, but the electronic components may become obsolete far sooner than the traditional mechanism. With most installations only a few years old, their lifetime costs remain uncertain. A seemingly inexpensive repair may eventually require replacement parts that nobody still manufactures.

The broader lesson concerns what preservation is intended to achieve. Restoring a historical object does not necessarily revive its original function or the habits of its former users. Equally, incorporating new technology does not automatically destroy authenticity. Councils need to explain not only what has been saved, but what compromises have been made.

items.prompt: Shifts in ambient ______ interfered with the precision of early clock mechanisms.
items.evidence: Temperature changes affected the movement of metal parts
items.reason: The cause is the environmental variation, not repair delays.

items.prompt: By the 1970s, many towers survived because of their ______ importance rather than their practical usefulness.
items.evidence: protected mainly for architectural reasons
items.reason: Historical buildings were retained even without their former public service.

items.prompt: A civic time display might benefit a passer-by whose phone has a flat ______.
items.evidence: whose phone battery is empty
items.reason: The question paraphrases empty as exhausted.

items.prompt: In one seaside location, airborne ______ had caused deterioration inside the original clockwork.
items.evidence: salt carried inland by sea air had corroded the metal gears
items.reason: The relevant material is not sea water as a whole.

items.prompt: The decision to conserve the working gears diverted public funding away from the local ______.
items.evidence: reduce funding available to the nearby library
items.reason: Identify the alternative public service receiving less funding.

items.prompt: The modern controls in a hybrid restoration may become ______ long before the traditional gears wear out.
items.evidence: components may become obsolete
items.reason: The statement is a possibility, not a certainty.

blocks.title: Supported sentence endings
blocks.mode: Withheld independent transfer continued; no scaffolds
blocks.instructions: Using the preceding passage, complete Questions 7–10 with endings A–G. Three endings are not used.

stimulus.title: Endings
paragraphs: A  because evidence showed that most local residents checked it frequently.
B  despite the loss of money that could otherwise support another municipal facility.
C  because restoring it had been shown to increase tourism and retail spending.
D  because the lifetime expense of the modern components has not yet been established.
E  despite evidence that hardly anyone could remember actually consulting it.
F  because specialist engineers would no longer be needed to maintain its mechanical parts.
G  even after its original usefulness as a public timekeeping service had faded.

items.prompt: Residents expressed affection for a restored clock
items.evidence: few remembered checking it during the previous week
items.reason: Residents' stated attachment contrasts with a survey showing few had checked the time recently. A reverses the survey's finding.

items.prompt: The heritage committee selected a costly traditional repair
items.evidence: reduce funding available to the nearby library
items.reason: The council's decision to preserve mechanical heritage reduced funds available for the library. F wrongly implies all maintenance ended.

items.prompt: The financial case for hybrid clock repairs remains uncertain
items.evidence: their lifetime costs remain uncertain
items.reason: Electronic controllers may reduce immediate maintenance but whole-life costs remain unproven; D preserves that uncertainty.

items.prompt: Many old clock towers were preserved for their appearance
items.evidence: protected mainly for architectural reasons
items.reason: Towers could survive as architectural landmarks even after practical timekeeping was no longer needed. C invents economic evidence.
